title: Cognitive Bias

source.name: Wikipedia — Cognitive bias
source.note: Đã rút gọn: chỉ giữ một số đoạn.

paras: A cognitive bias is a systematic pattern of deviation from the norm or rationality in judgment. Individuals create their own "subjective reality" from their perception of the input. An individual's construction of reality, not the objective input, may dictate their behavior in the world. Thus, cognitive biases may sometimes lead to perceptual distortion, inaccurate judgment, illogical interpretation, and irrationality.

While cognitive biases may initially appear to be negative, some are adaptive. They may lead to more effective actions in a given context. Furthermore, allowing cognitive biases enables faster decisions which can be desirable when timeliness is more valuable than accuracy, as illustrated in heuristics. Other cognitive biases are a "by-product" of human processing limitations, resulting from a lack of appropriate mental mechanisms (bounded rationality), the impact of an individual's constitution and biological state (embodied cognition), or simply from a limited capacity for information processing. Cognitive biases can make individuals more inclined to endorsing pseudoscientific beliefs by requiring less evidence for claims that confirm their preconceptions. This can potentially distort their perceptions and lead to inaccurate judgments.
When making judgments under uncertainty, people rely on mental shortcuts or heuristics, which provide swift estimates about the possibility of uncertain occurrences. For example,

the representativeness heuristic is defined as the tendency to judge the frequency or likelihood of an occurrence by the extent of which the event resembles the typical case. Similarly the availability heuristic is that individuals estimate the likelihood of events by how easy they are to recall, and the anchoring heuristic prefers the initial reference points that are recalled. While these heuristics are efficient and simple for the brain to compute, they sometimes introduce predictable and systematic cognitive errors, or biases.

The "Linda Problem" illustrates the representativeness heuristic and corresponding bias. Participants were given a description of "Linda" that suggests Linda might well be a feminist (e.g., she is said to be concerned about discrimination and social justice issues). They were then asked whether they thought Linda was more likely to be (a) a "bank teller" or (b) a "bank teller and active in the feminist movement". A majority chose answer (b). Independent of the information given about Linda, though, the more restrictive answer (b) is under any circumstance statistically less likely than answer (a). This is an example of the conjunction fallacy: respondents chose (b) because it seemed more "representative" or typical of persons who might fit the description of Linda. If they assumed that choosing (a) would entail Linda not being active in the feminist movement, that would be a pragmatic implicature. The representativeness heuristic may lead to errors such as activating stereotypes and inaccurate judgments of others.

Gerd Gigerenzer argues that heuristics should not lead us to conceive of human thinking as riddled with irrational cognitive biases. They should rather conceive rationality as an adaptive tool, not identical to the rules of formal logic or the probability calculus. Gigerenzer believes that cognitive biases are not biases, but rules of thumb, or as he would put it "gut feelings" that can actually help us make accurate decisions in our lives. There is not clear evidence that these behaviors are genuinely, severely biased once the actual problems people face are understood. Advances in economics and cognitive neuroscience now suggest that many behaviors previously labeled as biases might instead represent optimal decision-making strategies.

questions.q: What point is made about “subjective reality” in paragraph 1?
options: People react to their own reading of what they perceive, not to plain fact
People share one reality because they all receive the same input from outside
People change reality itself simply by thinking about it in a different way
People always see the world exactly as it is, with no distortion of any kind
questions.explain: Đoạn 1: mỗi người tạo “subjective reality” từ nhận thức; “construction of reality, not the objective input, may dictate their behavior”.

questions.q: Why does the writer say that allowing cognitive biases can sometimes be desirable?
options: They make sure that every judgment turns out to be completely accurate
They remove the need to look for evidence before making a choice
They help people to avoid feeling uncertain about any decision
They make quicker decisions possible when speed matters more than precision
questions.explain: Đoạn 2: cho phép thiên kiến giúp “faster decisions which can be desirable when timeliness is more valuable than accuracy”.

questions.q: What link does the text make between cognitive biases and pseudoscientific beliefs?
options: Biases only affect people who have received no scientific education
Biases can lead people to accept claims that fit their views on weaker evidence
Biases force people to demand more proof before they accept any claim
Pseudoscience is the main reason for the existence of cognitive biases
questions.explain: Đoạn 2: thiên kiến khiến con người dễ tin giả khoa học vì “requiring less evidence for claims that confirm their preconceptions”.

questions.q: Which situation is an example of the “availability heuristic”?
options: A student decides a quiet man must be a librarian because he fits the usual image
A woman judges a price by comparing it with the first price she was shown
A man thinks flying is very dangerous because plane crashes are easy to remember
A manager collects all the available data before she makes her decision
questions.explain: Đoạn 4: availability = ước lượng khả năng xảy ra theo mức độ dễ nhớ lại. Neo giá đầu tiên là anchoring; đoán nghề theo hình mẫu điển hình là representativeness.

questions.q: Why does the “Linda Problem” show an error in reasoning?
options: A combined description cannot be likelier than one part of it, yet most chose it
The description gave no hint that Linda was interested in social issues at all
The people who took part did not read the description of Linda with any care
Most people chose the answer that contained the smallest amount of information
questions.explain: Đoạn 5: phương án (b) “bank teller and active in the feminist movement” luôn ít khả năng hơn (a) “bank teller”; đa số vẫn chọn (b) vì nó “representative” hơn (conjunction fallacy).

questions.q: What is Gerd Gigerenzer’s view of heuristics?
options: They are the main reason why human thinking is irrational
Many so-called biases may actually be useful rules of thumb in real life
They have been proved to cause serious errors in most decisions
They should be replaced by the rules of formal logic
questions.explain: Đoạn 6: ông cho rằng đó là “rules of thumb… gut feelings” giúp quyết định chính xác; chưa có bằng chứng rõ ràng rằng chúng thực sự là thiên kiến nghiêm trọng.

questions.q: The text suggests that all cognitive biases are harmful.
questions.explain: Đoạn 2: “some are adaptive” – có thể dẫn đến hành động hiệu quả hơn; đoạn 6 còn đi xa hơn.

questions.q: The “Linda Problem” experiment was first carried out with university students.
questions.explain: Bài chỉ nói “Participants were given a description”, không nêu ai là người tham gia.
